content: The document titled Web Annex B: Updated Systematic Review of the Performance of Vaginal Discharge Syndromic Management in Treating Vaginal and Cervical Infections is part of the World Health Organization's (WHO) guidelines for managing symptomatic sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This systematic review and meta-analysis, published in June 2021, evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of syndromic management approaches for vaginal and cervical infections. The publication is available under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use with proper citation, but it does not imply WHO endorsement of specific organizations, products, or services. The systematic review updates a prior analysis by Zemouri et al. (2016) and includes studies published between January 2015 and September 2018. The review focuses on the diagnostic performance of vaginal discharge flowcharts compared to laboratory diagnostic tests. Studies were included if they provided data on sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) or allowed these parameters to be calculated. Studies that did not differentiate between cervical infections (caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis) and vaginal infections (caused by Trichomonas vaginalis and bacterial vaginosis) were excluded. Only studies published in English, French, Spanish, or Dutch were considered, and case reports or letters to the editor were excluded. The review categorized flowcharts into four types: 1. Flowchart 1: History and risk assessment. 2. Flowchart 2: History, risk assessment, and speculum examination. 3. Flowchart 3: History, risk assessment, speculum examination, and vaginal discharge samples analyzed via Gram staining and microscopy. 4. Flowchart 4: Country-adapted flowcharts or other combinations of screening methods. A meta-analysis was conducted by pooling data from studies using these flowcharts. If a study presented separate results for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, T. vaginalis, and bacterial vaginosis, the data with the highest PPV were included to avoid overrepresentation. The updated review identified 1,569 citations, of which 1,258 were screened after removing duplicates. Following title and abstract screening, 173 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and four new studies were included in the review. These studies, along with 16 from the previous review, brought the total to 20 studies. The four newly included studies involved 2,240 participants, while the previous review covered 10,538 participants. The review assessed the risk of bias in included studies using the QUADAS-2 tool, evaluating patient selection, index tests, reference standards, and flow/timing. The risk of bias varied across studies, with some showing high or unclear risks in specific domains. The findings highlight the diagnostic validity of different flowcharts for identifying cervical and vaginal infections. For example, one study (Barry 2018) validated a single flowchart for both cervical and vaginal infections, while others assessed specific flowcharts for individual infections. The pooled diagnostic performance of these flowcharts was analyzed to determine their effectiveness in clinical settings. This publication is part of WHO's broader guidelines for managing symptomatic STIs and aims to provide transparent and evidence-based recommendations. It emphasizes the importance of accurate diagnostic tools for improving the management of vaginal and cervical infections, particularly in resource-limited settings.
